newsitem.title: USA: Ill. Gov says encouraged by school funding talks.
newsitem.headline: Ill. Gov says encouraged by school funding talks.

text.p: Illinois Gov. Jim Edgar said Wednesday he has been encouraged by talks on school funding reforms, but fears that if legislators fail to act this session, they will not address financing disparities for several years.

Edgar has recommended increasing the Illinois income tax in order to provide local property tax relief and additional money to address funding disparities between districts in poor and affluent communities.

During a speech at the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago symposium on the Midwest economy, Edgar said he was pleased with the report's generally positive outlook for Illinois and the rest of the Midwest, but also said that school financing reform is important to future growth.
While "money alone" cannot guarantee quality education, minimum funding levels must be established to provide students with basic needs such as textbooks, Edgar said.

"Hopefully we will deal with it in the next five weeks in the Illinois General Assembly," Edgar said. "My fear is that if we don't deal with it in the next five weeks, we won't deal with it until well into the next century."
Legislative leaders have appointed eight representatives and senators to address the school financing issue and create a concrete proposal for the current session, scheduled to end in five weeks.
Following his speech, Edgar said he was "encouraged" by the response he received to his plan outline and said that the leaders are "working in the right direction" toward funding reforms.
The Chicago Fed on Wednesday released the results of a year-long study into the Midwest region economy in Illinois and followed the release with panel discussions.
The study concluded that the regional economy has prospered in recent years through its traditional agricultural and industrial bases.
To ensure continued growth, however, policymakers must foster training, tax incentives and new technologies, the study found.

Richard Mattoon, senior economist for the Chicago Fed, noted that the study found that general tax incentives are preferable to specific tax abatements or other arrangements in the longrun. Targeting property in distressed areas could reap real benefits as well, the study found.
Edgar also prefers general improvements rather than property specific incentives, he said.

MarySue Barrett, president of the Metropolitan Planning Council and a strong supporter of school finance reform, said the prognosis for reforms this session is "cloudy," but there is reason for optimism.
School funding reforms would result in property tax relief, which would also benefit Illinois businesses, Barrett said.
